analysis.one_liner: Bars ex-presidents, ex-vice presidents, ex-Members, and top appointees from lobbying for foreign governments for ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban former officials from foreign lobbying for ten years never got a House vote; it died in committee after a single member cosponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a criminal ten-year ban on former Presidents, Vice Presidents, Members of Congress, and senior presidential appointees representing or advising foreign governments before Congress or executive agencies. Violators would face fines and prison under existing criminal penalties for lobbying violations. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a crime subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would gain a check on the revolving door in which former top officials sell their access and influence to foreign governments. It would also protect the integrity of U.S. decisions on foreign policy, trade, and sanctions that are currently shaped behind the scenes by paid foreign agents who once held federal office.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens and U.S. policy independence

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal crime for former Presidents, Vice Presidents, Members of Congress, and Senate-confirmed appointees to lobby or advise a foreign government before any federal official for ten years after leaving office [S2] [S3].

It covers not just direct lobbying but also aiding or advising a foreign entity with the intent to influence U.S. officials, and includes entities owned or controlled by foreign governments, closing common workarounds [S3].
Violators face existing criminal penalties of fines and imprisonment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Former senior officials and the foreign-influence industry (law and lobbying firms that represent foreign governments) would lose a lucrative line of business. Anyone considering a move from government to foreign lobbying would face new legal risk.

drawbacks.text: A ten-year ban reaches far beyond the standard federal revolving-door limits (which are one to two years for most officials) and raises fair questions about whether a former Member of Congress can be criminally barred from a lawful profession, which courts may scrutinize under First Amendment speech and petition rights. This is a policy-design debate, not something the record settles.

The bill is narrow: it does nothing about domestic corporate lobbying by former officials, and it applies only to foreign governments and government-controlled entities, so lobbying for foreign-owned private companies would remain untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and simple: it stops former top officials from being paid to push foreign governments' agendas with their old colleagues. The main honest objection is the length of the ban and the breadth of covered positions; a shorter ban for less senior roles would still capture most of the problem with less constitutional risk. As written, the ban is aggressive but aimed squarely at a genuine conflict-of-interest channel.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee for the rest of the 112th Congress and never received a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Wolf introduced the bill on March 29, 2012, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On April 16, 2012, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where it stayed with no further action [S5].
Only one member cosponsored the bill, so it ended the Congress without any vote in either chamber [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former officials who cash in on foreign lobbying, and the law firms that arrange it, kept a revenue stream the bill would have closed; the House leadership and Judiciary Committee were never required to take a position.

for.name: Rep. Frank R. Wolf
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; recruited one cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's lone cosponsor was a fellow Republican, so the small support was intra-party and the outcome reflects inaction rather than a partisan split [S4].

industries.industry: Foreign-agent lobbying firms and law firms serving foreign governments
industries.note: The bill would cut off a lucrative practice: hiring former presidents, vice presidents, members of Congress, and top appointees to lobby or advise for foreign governments. Their interest in keeping the practice is directly at odds with citizens' interest in decisions not being influenced by paid foreign agents.

industries.industry: Former senior federal officials (Members of Congress, presidents, vice presidents, Senate-confirmed appointees)
industries.note: They would lose access to the foreign-government consulting market that monetizes their old offices and contacts for ten years after leaving service.
